subject: Chemistry
topic: The carboxyl group: structure and naming
title: The Carboxyl Group: Structure and Naming
summary: What –COOH really is: a carbonyl and a hydroxyl on one sp² carbon, joined by resonance that makes the carbon less electrophilic than in aldehydes; and how carboxylic acids get their common and IUPAC names.

notes.title: 14 – The Carboxyl Group: Structure and Naming

keyPoints: **–COOH** = a **carbonyl** (C=O) + a **hydroxyl** (–OH) on one carbon: carb-oxyl.
The carboxyl carbon is **sp²**: planar, bonds about **120°** apart.
**Resonance**: an –OH lone pair moves toward C while the C=O pair moves onto O, so the carbon is **less electrophilic** than in aldehydes and ketones (no nucleophilic addition).
**Common names** come from the source: formic (formica, ant), acetic (acetum, vinegar), butyric (butyrum, butter).
**IUPAC**: alkane − e + **oic acid**; the COOH carbon is C-1; two COOH groups keep the e (ethanedioic acid).

blocks.p: One curved arrow takes a lone pair of the –OH oxygen into the C–O bond; another takes the C=O π pair onto the carbonyl oxygen. The carbon's δ⁺ is partly made up, so it is **less electrophilic** than the carbonyl carbon of an aldehyde.

list: Replace the final **-e** of the alkane by **-oic acid**.
Two COOH groups: **keep the -e**, add **-dioic acid**.

quiz.q: The carboxyl group is made of:
Why is the carboxyl carbon less electrophilic than an aldehyde's carbonyl carbon?
quiz.explain: An –OH lone pair is delocalised toward the carbon, partly making up its δ⁺.

quiz.q: The IUPAC name of CH₃COOH is:
quiz.explain: Two carbons: ethane − e + oic acid.
With two COOH groups the -e of ethane is kept: ethane-dioic acid (oxalic acid).

quiz.q: Formic acid gets its name from:
quiz.explain: Latin formica = ant; ant stings contain formic acid.

simulation.reason: Structure and naming rules: the bond-line structures, the resonance arrows and the naming table carry them, and the quiz and workbook practise them. There is no variable to manipulate.
